title: Direction finding, contests and linking
blurb: How to hunt a transmitter, run a contest exchange, read a grid locator, and link repeaters over the internet.

T8C01.why: **Radio direction finding** locates where a signal comes from, including noise sources and jamming.
T8C01.trap: Radar-style techniques and echolocation aren't how ham signals are found.

T8C02.why: A hidden transmitter hunt needs a **directional antenna** to find the direction of the signal. SWR and power meters can't.

T8C03.why: **Contesting** is making as many contacts as possible in a set period.
T8C03.trap: Hidden transmitter hunts and nets are different activities.

T8C04.why: In a contest send **only your call sign and the required exchange**. Anything extra slows everyone.
T8C04.trap: Partial calls and duplicate contacts waste time.

T8C05.why: A grid locator is a **letter-number code for a geographic location**, such as FN31.
T8C05.trap: It isn't an instrument, and it isn't a direction or elevation.

T8C06.why: IRLP nodes are controlled over the air with **DTMF** keypad tones.
T8C06.trap: CTCSS tones just open a repeater's squelch.

T8C07.why: VoIP delivers **voice over the internet using digital techniques**.

T8C08.why: IRLP **connects amateur systems such as repeaters via the internet**.

T8C09.why: With **EchoLink** you can transmit through a repeater from a computer or phone, with no radio to start.
T8C09.trap: IRLP, D-STAR and DMR all start from a radio.

T8C10.why: Before using EchoLink, **register your call sign and provide proof of license**.
T8C10.trap: No training, purchase or General license is needed.

T8C11.why: A station that connects amateur stations to the internet is a **gateway**.
T8C11.trap: A repeater retransmits over radio only; a digipeater relays packets.
